newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin pushes for G8 but Japan wary.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin pushes for G8 but Japan wary.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, giving a confident "thumbs up" as he stepped off his plane, arrived at the summit of the Group of Seven leading nations on Thursday seeking full membership of the elite club for Russia.

But the 66-year-old Kremlin leader faced opposition before the three-day summit even began. Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said firmly that he did not want Russia to participate in all discussions.

"We are interested in seeing a consensus among G7 leaders that Russia will continue to be excluded from G7 talks on financial and macro-economic issues," Hashimoto told reporters as he flew to Denver.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky played down the disagreement and said Yeltsin, attending his fifth G7 summit, would be excluded from only one brief session on financial matters.

"In 11 hours of talks, there is only one hour during which the G8 will work without the participation of the Russian president, which for technical reasons are not yet of interest to Russia," he said.
"I do not think the Japanese position has changed in the time we were in the air."

Russia is not a formal member of G7 and Japan's reluctance to give Moscow a higher profile stems from a territorial dispute which has blocked the signing of a formal peace treaty after the Second World War. Tokyo wants the return of four islands seized by Soviet troops at the end of the war.

But Japanese officials in Denver played up recent signs of warmer relations and said Hashimoto was expected to accept an offer by Yeltsin to hold annual summits between the leaders of the two countries when the two men meet on Friday.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Yeltsin's friend and his closest ally in Europe, said the G7 would become a "Group of Eight" and that Russia would continue to participate in the annual summits.

Russia regards membership of the G7 -- the United States, Italy, Japan, Germany, Britain, France and Canada -- as a way to underline its democratic and economic progress since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
Yeltsin, who is accompanied by reform chief Anatoly Chubais and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, smiled broadly and waved as he arrived in Denver.
He lost weight during almost eight months out of the Kremlin with heart problems and his return after heart surgery on November 5 was set back by a bout of pneumonia.

Yeltsin is now seeking Russian membership of the Paris Club of creditor nations. Russian officials say this could help indebted Moscow win back funds lent to the Soviet Union's former allies in the developing countries and the communist world.
"This is one of the basic aims of the Russian delegation," Yastrzhembsky told reporters.
Russia also wants to join the World Trade Organisation and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, but acknowledges that negotiations will take time.
